title: The integration of virtual reality and EEG: A step-by-step guideline
author: Krampe, Wolfers, et al.

steps.title: Check hardware specifications
steps.instruction: Confirm that the following hardware is available and meets the minimum or recommended specifications: Varjo XR3 PC‑VR headset with eye‑tracking, Neuroelectrics Enobio 32‑channel EEG system (recorded with NIC2 software v2.1.3.6), and a desktop PC (example: Alienware Aurora Ryzen Edition R14 running Windows 10 22H2, AMD Ryzen 9 5900 12‑core CPU, 64 GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU with 24 GB VRAM). Minimum PC requirements (per Varjo/Neuroelectrics) are an 8‑core CPU (Intel i7‑9700K or AMD Ryzen 7 2700X), 32 GB DDR4/DDR5 RAM, GPU at least NVIDIA RTX 3070/2080 Ti, 2 GB storage, 2× DisplayPort 1.4, 2× USB‑A 3.0/3.1, and Windows 10 64‑bit (or Windows 11). Recommended specs are a premium 8‑core CPU (Intel i9‑9900K, Xeon W‑2245, or AMD Ryzen 7 3700X), GPU NVIDIA RTX 4070Ti/3080/RTX 6000 Ada/A6000, and the same RAM and OS.

steps.title: Install Unity and required packages
steps.instruction: Install Unity 2022.3.28f1 with Unity Hub 3.8.0. In Unity’s Package Manager enable the OpenXR Plugin (version ≥ 1.10.0) and the XR Interaction Toolkit (version ≥ 2.5.3). Add the Varjo Unity XR SDK Plugin from Varjo’s GitHub and ensure the Varjo XR Plugin checkbox is ticked in Project Settings → XR Plugin Management → Varjo. Install Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) version 1.16.0 and the LSL4Unity package (add via Window → Package Manager → Add package from git URL). Verify that a Varjo XR subscription (monthly or lifetime) is active. Ensure the PC meets the software requirements listed in Table 2 (Unity ≥ 2021.3 LTS, OpenXR ≥ 1.10.0, Varjo Base ≥ 4.7.0, Enobio firmware 4021, NIC2 ≥ 2.1.3.11).

steps.title: Configure Unity XR project
steps.instruction: Create or open the Unity VR project that already runs in Play mode with an OpenXR rig. Add the Varjo Unity XR SDK Plugin and enable it. Import the Varjo eye‑tracking template script (EyeTrackingExample.cs) from the official Varjo Git repository. Add collider components (mesh or box) to every virtual object of interest (e.g., sustainability labels on tea packages) and give each collider a unique, meaningful name that will appear in the data log. Add three transform objects – fixation point, left eye, right eye – and a gaze‑point indicator to the scene (these are included in the OpenXR prefab or the sample scene). Assign these objects to the corresponding fields in the eye‑tracking script via the Inspector. Place the modified EyeTrackingExample.cs on an empty GameObject in the hierarchy and configure its Inspector settings (e.g., set the logging key to F2).

steps.title: Set up eye‑tracking logging
steps.instruction: Modify the Varjo template so that the gaze‑raycast logs a collider‑based hit: when the gaze ray collides with a named GameObject, the script writes a new column ‘HitObjectName’ together with ‘CaptureTime’ (sampled at ~200 frames / second) to the output CSV. Ensure the collider’s size is adjusted with the Edit Collider function if needed. Confirm that the script’s key (default F2) starts eye‑tracking logging when pressed during Play mode. Verify that the output file contains timestamps, HitObjectName, and CaptureTime for synchronisation with EEG and behavioural data.

steps.title: Integrate EEG via Lab Streaming Layer
steps.instruction: Add the LSL4Unity package (git URL) to the Unity project. In Unity, create an LSL outlet that sends event markers (e.g., identifier ‘FavoriteProductGrabbing’ followed by a formatted string containing timestamp, event type, trial number, left/right package info) whenever the OnObjectGrabbed function from the OpenXR Interaction Toolkit is triggered. Configure the NIC2 software (Neuroelectrics Enobio, version 2.1.3.6) to act as an LSL inlet streaming EEG data (8 electrodes: Fp1, Fp2, Fpz, AF7, AF8, C3, C4, Cz) at 500 Hz, with ground DRL and reference CMS placed behind the left ear using Kendall H124SG electrodes and Signagel cap. Ensure LSL receives both the EEG stream and the Unity event stream, and that data are saved to three files: a .csv for experiment events, a .csv for eye‑tracking data, and a .mat file for EEG data.

steps.title: Prepare EEG cap and electrodes
steps.instruction: Fit the Enobio cap using a size that centres Cz relative to nasion, inion, and the tops of the ears. Place eight scalp electrodes (Fp1, Fp2, Fpz, AF7, AF8, C3, C4, Cz) with conductive gel for good signal quality. Attach the ground electrode (DRL) and reference electrode (CMS) behind the left ear on the mastoid bone using Kendall H124SG single‑use electrodes. Verify signal quality in NIC2 before proceeding.

steps.title: Perform experiment and record data
steps.instruction: Follow this exact sequence: 1) Power on the PC, log in, and launch Unity, LSL, and NIC2. 2) Place the EEG cap on the participant, check signal quality, then disconnect the EEG amplifier to allow the VR headset to be mounted. 3) Prepare the Varjo XR3 headset, start the Varjo Base software, power the base stations, and launch SteamVR (outside‑in tracking with Valve Index controllers). The headset automatically runs eye‑tracking calibration. 4) Re‑connect the EEG amplifier, re‑open NIC2, and confirm signal quality again. 5) Open LSL on the PC, configure it to receive the Unity event outlet and the NIC2 EEG inlet, and start EEG recording in NIC2. 6) After eye‑tracking calibration, press F2 (or the configured key) to begin eye‑tracking logging, then press Play in Unity to start the VR experiment. The OnObjectGrabbed function will log experiment events, send LSL markers, and write to the three data files. Monitor that timestamps, HitObjectName, and EEG samples are being recorded synchronously.

steps.title: Stop recording and shut down
steps.instruction: When the experiment is finished, first stop EEG recording in NIC2, then remove the VR headset, stop Unity’s Play mode, and finally stop the LSL streams (LSL should be the last component shut down). Ensure all data files are saved and backed up.
